title: Rate-Utility Frontiers for Language Encodings: Comparing Tokens, Bytes, and Pixels
hook: Tokens, bytes, or pixels — which encodes language best? A controlled head-to-head across 13 languages finds no single winner: each encoding trades off differently by task.
key_points: Controls for content and downstream capacity together, using a shared bottleneck swept in width to trace rate-utility frontiers.
Tested across 13 languages and 5 scripts, on 3 utilities: surface-form preservation, cross-lingual alignment, and topic classification.
Pixels preserve surface form best; bytes preserve cross-lingual alignment best (especially within the same script); tokens win at topic prediction.
No single encoding dominates across tasks or capacity regimes — the tradeoff is real, not an artifact of sequence length.
Short inputs can lose useful meaning while long inputs can still compress well, so length alone doesn't explain the differences.
content_html: Language models can represent text as subword tokens, raw bytes, or even rendered pixels — but comparisons between these choices are usually confounded, since each exposes a different amount of linguistic content per language. This paper strips that confound out.
extra_html:
Ingo Ziegler, Desmond Elliott, and Martin Krebs use verified parallel sentences across thirteen languages and five scripts, passing tokens, bytes, and pixels through a shared bottleneck whose width is swept to trace out rate-utility frontiers. That setup separates three things normally conflated: how many input positions an encoding creates, how much latent capacity survives encoding, and how much task-relevant information survives compression. They then score three utilities — surface-form preservation, cross-lingual sentence alignment, and topic classification.

The headline finding is that no encoding wins everywhere: pixels are best at preserving exact surface form, bytes are best at cross-lingual alignment (especially within the same script), and tokens are best for topic prediction. The authors stress this isn't just about sequence length — short inputs can lose meaning while long ones can still compress well — so choosing an encoding is a genuine rate-utility tradeoff shaped by task, language mix, capacity, and compute budget. arXiv, July 2026.

related.title: Subword Tokenization with Byte-Pair Encoding
related.hook: Whole words make a giant vocabulary; single characters make long sequences. Subwords split the difference — and let models read words they've never seen.

related.title: SentencePiece: Language-Independent Tokenization
related.hook: Most tokenizers assume you can split on spaces first. SentencePiece drops that assumption and tokenizes raw text directly — in any language.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean to compare encodings 'under a shared bottleneck'?
flashcards.back_html: The authors route tokens, bytes, and pixels through a compression bottleneck of swept width, separating input length, latent capacity, and task-relevant information — quantities usually conflated.

flashcards.prompt: Which encoding won on which utility, per the paper?

choices.text: Pixels best for surface form, bytes best for cross-lingual alignment, tokens best for topic classification

flashcards.explanation_html: No encoding dominates overall — pixels preserve surface form best, bytes preserve cross-lingual sentence alignment best, and tokens best support topic prediction.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't you explain the encoding differences by sequence length alone?
flashcards.back_html: Short inputs can discard useful meaning, while longer inputs can still compress well and preserve information — length alone doesn't predict which encoding wins.
